strengths: Addresses an important infrastructure problem for multilingual NLP. The broad Wikipedia audit and separate reporting of document and character removal provide useful evidence about resource availability beyond raw article counts.

Concrete examples establish the existence of duplicated placeholders, templated articles, and foreign-script contamination. The correlation between MinHash removal and independently estimated bot content (ρ = 0.63) supports the interpretation that deduplication detects repetitive, automatically generated material.

The experimental coverage is substantial: monolingual pretraining across 50 languages, XLM-R adaptation, multilingual pretraining, and several downstream tasks. Five-run results and a random-subsampling comparison strengthen parts of the evaluation. Cebuano’s SIB200 improvement from 0.39 to 0.51 demonstrates that filtering can provide meaningful benefits.

The paper is generally well organized, supplies extensive per-language results and training hyperparameters, and links an open-source filtering toolkit. Reporting adverse outcomes such as the Acehnese degradation is valuable.
weaknesses: The central quality taxonomy exceeds its validation. Filtering susceptibility is treated as evidence that removed content is low quality, culminating in the claim that approximately 30% of documents are low quality. However, Appendix A explicitly removes foreign-script names and references, while legitimate templated articles can contain distinct facts. Same-script contamination remains undetected. Correlations with bot prevalence and DEPTH+ (ρ = 0.31) do not establish linguistic quality. A stratified human audit of retained and removed material, including false-positive estimates and threshold sensitivity, is needed to substantiate the tiers.

The multilingual BELEBELE evaluation does not demonstrate preservation of useful reading-comprehension ability. Table 14 reports an average accuracy of 0.25 for both conditions, matching chance on this four-choice task; even English scores only 0.25–0.26. Small differences around this floor cannot support the interpretation offered in Section 5.3. The fine-tuning and evaluation setup needs validation against a functioning baseline. Table 12 also places the unadapted and raw-adapted XLM-R averages at chance, warranting investigation.

The random control matches article counts rather than token volume, although filtering disproportionately removes short and repetitive documents. It therefore does not adequately isolate quality from quantity. Appendix C additionally changes tokenizers between conditions and uses fixed epochs for monolingual training and adaptation, producing different training exposure. These choices permit an end-to-end pipeline comparison but weaken attribution to content quality. Token-matched controls and targeted ablations separating tokenization, script filtering, and deduplication would resolve this.

The claims of negligible degradation and greater benefits for lower-quality editions need stronger statistical support. Differences within ±0.05 are declared small without an equivalence criterion. Table 7 shows Tier 3 averages decreasing from 0.67 to 0.66 and Tier 4 remaining at 0.51, alongside substantial individual gains and losses. Table 13 shows average XNLI performance decreasing from 0.44 to 0.43. BELEBELE and multilingual results lack reported uncertainty, limiting conclusions about preservation and tier-dependent benefits.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the toolkit link and hyperparameter tables. The manuscript does not specify the Wikipedia dump date and extraction pipeline, MinHash shingle representation and LSH configuration, or the exact English multiple-choice training data denoted as 'MC'. Validation-split construction and the scope of repeated runs are also unclear. These details directly affect the audit statistics and downstream comparisons. Together with the validation concerns above, they require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.
